New technology does not automatically leave old inequalities behind. AI can reproduce the biases in the data, assumptions and decisions used to build it. If women’s needs and experiences are left out, we risk repeating the same mistakes—continuing to embed bias in the systems that shape work, opportunity and everyday life. We must not let this happen again and we must participate in how those systems are built, used, and held accountable. So why should women engage and participate with AI when we are already so busy? Use it better. Take your career further.From “ARGH, WTF?” to “Ah. That’s why.”What you ask, what context you provide, what the system can see and how you evaluate its answer can all change the result. Understand why an AI tool has gone off track—and what you can do about it. These are practical career skills: strengthening your work, exercising judgment and preparing for new responsibilities. See through the noise. Make sound decisions.From “OMG, the end is nigh!” to “Ugh, as if.”You cannot cut through that noise by memorising a list of approved opinions. You need enough of the fundamentals to ask: What evidence supports the claim? What does the demonstration leave out? What would have to be true for this prediction to happen? That is how you evaluate a tool, a workplace proposal or a headline on its merits. Have a say. Help change the defaults.From “Whatever” to “RSVP: Yes. I have notes!”Once you understand how AI works, you can participate meaningfully in decisions about what happens next. These debates are already happening—in workplaces, governments, schools, city halls and homes. Refusing to engage does not stop decisions from being made. It only means they will be made without you. Read why this matters in AI Fundamentals 101 → Women have always been pivotal to AI Meet the women behind AI and get inspired to help shape the future. “Computing is too important to be left to men.”— Karen Spärck Jones Women have shaped computing from its earliest foundations and helped build the ideas, machines and methods that made modern AI possible. What it becomes next is being decided right now. Getting involved—learning it, using it, having opinions about it—is how we shape the future the way we shaped the past. That is why LAiDIES exists. And since we’re here anyway, we may as well have fun. So join LAiDIES and make sure women continue to light the way. New technology does not automatically leave old inequalities behind. AI can reproduce the biases in the data, assumptions and decisions used to build it. If women’s needs and experiences are left out, we risk repeating the same mistakes—continuing to embed bias in the systems that shape work, opportunity and everyday life. We must not let this happen again and we must participate in how those systems are built, used, and held accountable. So why should women engage and participate with AI when we are already so busy? Use it better. Take your career further.From “ARGH, WTF?” to “Ah. That’s why.”What you ask, what context you provide, what the system can see and how you evaluate its answer can all change the result. Understand why an AI tool has gone off track—and what you can do about it. These are practical career skills: strengthening your work, exercising judgment and preparing for new responsibilities. See through the noise. Make sound decisions.From “OMG, the end is nigh!” to “Ugh, as if.”You cannot cut through that noise by memorising a list of approved opinions. You need enough of the fundamentals to ask: What evidence supports the claim? What does the demonstration leave out? What would have to be true for this prediction to happen? That is how you evaluate a tool, a workplace proposal or a headline on its merits. Have a say. Help change the defaults.From “Whatever” to “RSVP: Yes. I have notes!”Once you understand how AI works, you can participate meaningfully in decisions about what happens next. These debates are already happening—in workplaces, governments, schools, city halls and homes. Refusing to engage does not stop decisions from being made. It only means they will be made without you. What it becomes next is being decided right now. Getting involved—learning it, using it, having opinions about it—is how we shape the future the way we shaped the past. That is why LAiDIES exists. And since we’re here anyway, we may as well have fun. So join LAiDIES and make sure women continue to light the way. New technology does not automatically leave old inequalities behind. AI can reproduce the biases in the data, assumptions and decisions used to build it. If women’s needs and experiences are left out, we risk repeating the same mistakes—continuing to embed bias in the systems that shape work, opportunity and everyday life. We must not let this happen again and we must participate in how those systems are built, used, and held accountable. So why should women engage and participate with AI when we are already so busy? That’s why.”What you ask, what context you provide, what the system can see and how you evaluate its answer can all change the result. Understand why an AI tool has gone off track—and what you can do about it. These are practical career skills: strengthening your work, exercising judgment and preparing for new responsibilities. See through the noise. Make sound decisions.From “OMG, the end is nigh!” to “Ugh, as if.”You cannot cut through that noise by memorising a list of approved opinions. You need enough of the fundamentals to ask: What evidence supports the claim? What does the demonstration leave out? What would have to be true for this prediction to happen? That is how you evaluate a tool, a workplace proposal or a headline on its merits. Have a say. Help change the defaults.From “Whatever” to “RSVP: Yes. I have notes!”Once you understand how AI works, you can participate meaningfully in decisions about what happens next. These debates are already happening—in workplaces, governments, schools, city halls and homes. Refusing to engage does not stop decisions from being made. It only means they will be made without you.
